elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在突出在资源有限且主要关注埃博拉病毒病(EVD)的埃博拉病毒病治疗中心(ETU)中管理破裂异位妊娠的挑战。背景强调异位妊娠是一种产科急症,需要早期诊断以确保母体生存。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究描述了一名30多岁的孕妇因疑似埃博拉病毒病(EVD)被送往刚果民主共和国(DRC)的ETU。她13个月前曾从埃博拉病毒感染中康复,入院时表现为停经8周和盆腔疼痛。
elements_zh.methods: 患者使用邻近卫生中心的一个未使用的建筑进行探索性剖腹探查,以确认破裂异位妊娠。在入院后48小时和72小时进行了埃博拉病毒病的实时聚合酶链反应(RT-PCR)检测,结果均为阴性。
elements_zh.main_results: 患者出现了出血性休克,并被诊断为左侧输卵管破裂异位妊娠。入院后48小时和72小时进行的埃博拉病毒病实时聚合酶链反应(RT-PCR)检测结果均为阴性,确认其在就诊时未感染埃博拉病毒病(EVD)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为在ETU中发生的破裂异位妊娠病例,强调了处理产科急症资源不足的问题。该病例具有新颖性,因为它是在ETU环境中首次报告的此类并发症。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,ETU需要具备足够的能力来处理不仅埃博拉病毒病,还包括其他可能在资源有限环境中出现的产科并发症。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于单一病例报告,可能不具备普遍适用性。证据强度中等,因为它基于ETU内的临床观察和诊断程序,没有进行统计分析或更广泛的人群数据研究。

papers.abstract_zh: 背景 异位妊娠(EP)是一种产科急症;早期诊断对于母体生存至关重要。在资源有限的环境中,如埃博拉病毒病治疗中心(ETU),延迟诊断或管理异位妊娠常导致破裂和危及生命的出血性休克。病例报告 我们报告了一名30多岁孕妇的病例,她因疑似埃博拉病毒病(EVD)被送往刚果民主共和国(DRC)的ETU。她的临床表现包括发热和腹痛,这些症状在入院前4天开始。13个月前,她曾从埃博拉病毒感染中康复。入院时,她表现为停经8周和间歇性盆腔疼痛。阴道检查发现子宫略大,可触及左侧附件区小肿块。实验室检查确认了疟疾和妊娠,其埃博拉病毒病(EVD)检测结果为阴性。由于ETU内没有超声波机,无法进行盆腔超声检查。随即开始支持性治疗。入院19小时后,患者出现急性外科腹部症状,表现为逐渐加重的左侧盆腔疼痛、腹部膨胀和弥漫性压痛。怀疑为破裂异位妊娠,并通过诊断性腹腔穿刺确认,发现腹腔内有血液。患者出现了出血性休克。然而,ETU缺乏手术室、手术设备和麻醉药物。由于没有具备手术能力的设施,无法将患者转至其他ETU;而转至社区医疗机构则需要在首次检测后48小时进行第二次阴性埃博拉病毒病检测。我们利用邻近卫生中心的一个未使用的建筑进行探索性剖腹探查,发现左侧输卵管异位妊娠并伴有壶腹部脱位和活动性出血。我们进行了左侧输卵管切除术并实施了止血缝合。入院后48小时和72小时进行的埃博拉病毒病实时聚合酶链反应(RT-PCR)检测结果均为阴性。患者术后恢复良好,于手术后第14天从ETU转至社区医疗机构。结论 破裂异位妊娠(REP)仍然是一个危及生命的产科急症,可能在资源有限且主要关注埃博拉病毒病(EVD)的ETU中发生。为保护母体健康,ETU不仅应确保对埃博拉病毒感染的适当治疗,还应具备及时诊断和处理产科并发症的能力。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为在ETU中发生的破裂异位妊娠病例,强调了处理产科急症资源不足的问题。该病例具有新颖性,因为它是在ETU环境中首次报告的此类并发症。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,ETU需要具备足够的能力来处理不仅埃博拉病毒病,还包括其他可能在资源有限环境中出现的产科并发症。

papers.title: When faith and biomedicine collide
papers.abstract: This chapter examines conflicts between faith- and biomedicine-based approaches to health, illness, and death during infectious disease outbreaks. Using a case-based and context-informed approach, we show the crucial contribution bioethics can make to resolving tensions and finding common ground. Section 5.1 introduces a case involving traditional burial practices in Sierra Leone during the Ebola virus disease outbreak. Section 5.2 considers a case in Uganda during the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)/acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) epidemic involving religiously driven efforts to substitute abstinence-only initiatives for evidence-based methods. Section 5.3 explores a case of vaccine refusal at a witch community in the North East region of Ghana during the novel coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Throughout the case analyses, the chapter develops and illustrates ethical principles of civility, change from within, epistemic justice, and equal respect. We show how these principles orient public health workers to ethically bridge differences and effectively safeguard health and life. The chapter concludes (in Section 5.4) with a bid for greater engagement of bioethics at the crossroads of biomedical and faith-based understandings of health and disease.

analysis.summary_en: This chapter explores the ethical challenges that arise when faith-based and biomedical approaches to health and illness conflict during infectious disease outbreaks. It uses case studies from Sierra Leone, Uganda, and Ghana to illustrate these tensions. The study highlights the importance of bioethics in mediating these conflicts and promoting ethical practices that respect both biomedical and faith-based perspectives. The chapter emphasizes the need for civility, epistemic justice, and equal respect in public health work. However, the analysis is based on case-based and context-informed approaches, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. The evidence suggests that ethical principles can guide public health workers in navigating these complex situations, but the study does not provide quantitative results or statistical analyses.

papers.abstract_zh: 本章探讨在传染病暴发期间,基于信仰与生物医学的健康、疾病与死亡观之间的冲突。通过基于病例与情境的分析方法,我们展示了生命伦理学在化解紧张局势、寻找共同立场方面的关键作用。第5.1节介绍塞拉利昂在埃博拉病毒病 暴发期间传统葬礼习俗的一个案例。第5.2节探讨乌干达在人类免疫缺陷病毒(HIV)/获得性免疫缺陷综合征(AIDS)流行期间,宗教驱动的仅禁欲倡议替代循证方法的案例。第5.3节分析加纳东北地区某巫术社区在2019新型冠状病毒(COVID-19)大流行期间疫苗拒绝的案例。在整个案例分析中,本章构建并阐释了文明、内部变革、认识论正义与平等尊重等伦理原则。我们展示这些原则如何引导公共卫生工作者在伦理层面跨越差异,有效保障健康与生命。第5.4节(结论)呼吁在生物医学与信仰驱动的健康与疾病观交汇处加强生命伦理学参与。

papers.full_text: Subjects The ongoing Ebola virus outbreak in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), declared a Public Health Emergency by the World Health Organization (WHO) on 17 May 2026, is set against a broader humanitarian crisis1. Armed conflict, mass displacement and reduced humanitarian funding are undermining disease surveillance, prevention and treatment not only for Ebola but also for malaria, tuberculosis (TB) and HIV, creating a syndemic that threatens years of progress in disease control. With more than 7 million internally displaced individuals and deteriorating health infrastructure, the region’s capacity to respond to outbreaks is critically weakened2,3. Disruptions to health services and access to safe water fuel the spread of epidemic-prone diseases while limiting access to diagnosis and treatment. Recent cuts in humanitarian assistance have exacerbated the situation by disrupting essential functions such as epidemic surveillance and medicine procurement4,5, jeopardizing programs for malaria and TB and threatening increased morbidity and mortality. Therefore, the current Ebola outbreak should be viewed as part of a larger syndemic driven by conflict and humanitarian retrenchment. Effective epidemic preparedness in eastern DRC requires integrated strategies to strengthen health-system resilience while maintaining critical programs for malaria, TB and HIV. Without sustained investment, the vulnerabilities of one of the world’s most fragile health systems will remain exposed and exacerbated. Conflict and humanitarian funding cuts threaten far more than the Ebola response; they increasingly disrupt essential malaria, TB and HIV services in eastern DRC. Insecurity damages health facilities, weakens supply chains, and interrupts diagnosis, treatment and follow-up, increasing preventable deaths and disease transmission. Malaria remains a leading cause of illness and death, particularly among children and displaced populations. Conflict has reduced access to insecticide-treated nets, rapid diagnostic tests and effective treatment, while untreated malaria complicates Ebola surveillance because the two diseases present with similar symptoms6. TB and HIV programs face similar disruptions. Interrupted access to diagnostics, medicines and community-based care increases treatment failure, mortality and drug resistance, especially among displaced populations7,8. Humanitarian funding reductions have further weakened procurement of medicines, diagnostics and vaccination services, threatening recent gains in disease control4,5. Conflict-related sexual violence also increases vulnerability to HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, while reductions in humanitarian services limit access to post-exposure prophylaxis, reproductive healthcare and psychosocial support9. Overall, the collapse of one part of the health system undermines multiple infectious disease programs. Ebola, malaria, TB and HIV require integrated responses that address both the impact of conflict and chronic underfunding to sustain disease control. The current crisis in eastern DRC highlights the limitations of disease-specific emergency responses in settings where multiple health threats interact simultaneously. A sustainable response requires a shift from reactive outbreak control toward strengthening the underlying health system that supports prevention, diagnosis and treatment across diseases. Addressing priorities is essential to prevent further deterioration of epidemic control. First, protecting healthcare delivery in conflict settings must be considered a core component of epidemic preparedness. Attacks on health facilities, healthcare workers and humanitarian personnel disrupt surveillance, vaccination, clinical care and outbreak response activities. Ensuring safe access for health workers and protecting medical infrastructure are essential obligations under international humanitarian law and should remain a priority for national authorities, armed actors and international partners4,10. Without functional health facilities, even well-funded epidemic responses cannot achieve timely detection, isolation and treatment. Second, humanitarian financing must be restored through flexible, sustained mechanisms that support both emergency response and routine health services. Short-term, disease-specific funding models are insufficient in protracted crises in which communities simultaneously face multiple infectious threats. Donors should prioritize financing approaches that allow rapid adaptation to changing epidemiological conditions while maintaining essential programs for malaria, TB, HIV, immunization and maternal health5,6. Investments should strengthen existing national and local health structures rather than creating parallel systems that are difficult to sustain after external support declines. Third, integrated disease surveillance and service delivery should replace fragmented vertical approaches. The same communities and health facilities are managing overlapping risks from Ebola, malaria, TB and HIV, yet these programs are often organized separately. Integrating community health workers, laboratory platforms, surveillance systems and supply chains would improve efficiency and increase resilience during future outbreaks. Lessons from the 2018–2020 Ebola response in eastern DRC demonstrated that community engagement, trust-building and locally adapted interventions are essential for improving acceptance of public health measures and maintaining continuity of care9. Fourth, reliable access to essential medicines and diagnostics must be guaranteed through stronger supply-chain systems. Stock-outs of antimalarial medicines, TB drugs, antiretroviral therapy, rapid diagnostic tests and personal protective equipment can rapidly transform manageable diseases into public health emergencies. Establishing strategic buffer stocks, improving procurement transparency and strengthening last-mile distribution systems in conflict-affected areas are critical measures to prevent treatment interruptions and dependence on informal medicine markets5,6,7,8. Beyond immediate interventions, eastern DRC needs a broader approach to epidemic preparedness based on resilient primary healthcare systems that can sustain essential services during conflict and displacement. Protecting routine health programs is therefore a cornerstone of outbreak preparedness. The syndemic in eastern DRC highlights the interdependence of humanitarian crises and infectious diseases. Effective epidemic control requires integrated strategies that strengthen health services, ensure sustainable financing, improve surveillance and maintain access to essential medicines and supplies. The Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC underscores a syndemic in which conflict disrupts the control of multiple diseases like malaria and HIV. A resilient health system is essential for effective epidemic preparedness. Long-term investment in healthcare infrastructure is crucial to prevent future health crises and break the cycle of recurring outbreaks. References - World Health Organization. Addressing priorities is essential to prevent further deterioration of epidemic control. First, protecting healthcare delivery in conflict settings must be considered a core component of epidemic preparedness. Attacks on health facilities, healthcare workers and humanitarian personnel disrupt surveillance, vaccination, clinical care and outbreak response activities. Ensuring safe access for health workers and protecting medical infrastructure are essential obligations under international humanitarian law and should remain a priority for national authorities, armed actors and international partners4,10. Without functional health facilities, even well-funded epidemic responses cannot achieve timely detection, isolation and treatment. Second, humanitarian financing must be restored through flexible, sustained mechanisms that support both emergency response and routine health services. Short-term, disease-specific funding models are insufficient in protracted crises in which communities simultaneously face multiple infectious threats. Donors should prioritize financing approaches that allow rapid adaptation to changing epidemiological conditions while maintaining essential programs for malaria, TB, HIV, immunization and maternal health5,6. Investments should strengthen existing national and local health structures rather than creating parallel systems that are difficult to sustain after external support declines. Third, integrated disease surveillance and service delivery should replace fragmented vertical approaches. The same communities and health facilities are managing overlapping risks from Ebola, malaria, TB and HIV, yet these programs are often organized separately. Integrating community health workers, laboratory platforms, surveillance systems and supply chains would improve efficiency and increase resilience during future outbreaks. Lessons from the 2018–2020 Ebola response in eastern DRC demonstrated that community engagement, trust-building and locally adapted interventions are essential for improving acceptance of public health measures and maintaining continuity of care9. Fourth, reliable access to essential medicines and diagnostics must be guaranteed through stronger supply-chain systems. Stock-outs of antimalarial medicines, TB drugs, antiretroviral therapy, rapid diagnostic tests and personal protective equipment can rapidly transform manageable diseases into public health emergencies. Establishing strategic buffer stocks, improving procurement transparency and strengthening last-mile distribution systems in conflict-affected areas are critical measures to prevent treatment interruptions and dependence on informal medicine markets5,6,7,8. Beyond immediate interventions, eastern DRC needs a broader approach to epidemic preparedness based on resilient primary healthcare systems that can sustain essential services during conflict and displacement. Protecting routine health programs is therefore a cornerstone of outbreak preparedness. The syndemic in eastern DRC highlights the interdependence of humanitarian crises and infectious diseases. Effective epidemic control requires integrated strategies that strengthen health services, ensure sustainable financing, improve surveillance and maintain access to essential medicines and supplies. The Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC underscores a syndemic in which conflict disrupts the control of multiple diseases like malaria and HIV. A resilient health system is essential for effective epidemic preparedness. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the impact of armed conflict and humanitarian funding cuts on the control of infectious diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis (TB) and HIV in eastern DRC, highlighting the broader implications for public health beyond the Ebola virus outbreak.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a descriptive analysis of the ongoing humanitarian and health crisis in eastern DRC, focusing on the effects of conflict and funding reductions on disease surveillance, prevention and treatment programs for Ebola, malaria, TB and HIV.
analysis.methods: The study uses qualitative and quantitative data from reports and analyses of the humanitarian situation in eastern DRC, including statistics on displaced populations, health infrastructure damage and service disruptions, to evaluate the impact on disease control programs.
analysis.main_results: Humanitarian funding cuts have disrupted essential functions such as epidemic surveillance and medicine procurement, jeopardizing programs for malaria and TB and threatening increased morbidity and mortality. Stock-outs of antimalarial medicines, TB drugs, antiretroviral therapy, rapid diagnostic tests and personal protective equipment can rapidly transform manageable diseases into public health emergencies.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as evidence that the current Ebola outbreak is part of a larger syndemic driven by conflict and humanitarian retrenchment, emphasizing the need for integrated responses to address multiple health threats simultaneously.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for integrated strategies to strengthen health-system resilience and ensure sustained investment in disease control programs, particularly in conflict-affected regions where multiple infectious diseases interact.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on reported data and does not include direct empirical measurements or statistical analyses. The evidence is moderate, based on observational data and implications from existing reports.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the impact of armed conflict and humanitarian funding cuts on the control of infectious diseases in eastern DRC, highlighting how these factors undermine disease surveillance, prevention and treatment for Ebola, malaria, tuberculosis and HIV. It emphasizes the broader public health implications, noting that the current Ebola outbreak is part of a larger syndemic driven by conflict and underfunding. The authors argue that integrated strategies are necessary to strengthen health systems and address multiple threats simultaneously. However, the study relies on observational data and does not include direct empirical measurements, limiting the strength of its evidence to moderate. The findings underscore the importance of restoring humanitarian financing and ensuring access to essential health services in conflict-affected areas.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨武装冲突与人道主义资金削减对刚果民主共和国东部地区疟疾、结核病与艾滋病等传染病防控的影响,并强调超越 埃博拉病毒 暴发 的公共卫生更广泛影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为一项针对刚果民主共和国东部地区人道主义与健康危机的描述性分析,重点关注冲突与资金减少对埃博拉、疟疾、结核病与艾滋病疾病 监测、预防与 治疗 项目的影响。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究采用定性与定量数据,来源于刚果民主共和国东部地区人道主义局势的报告与分析,包括流离失所人群统计、医疗基础设施损坏与服务中断等数据,以评估其对疾病防控项目的影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 人道主义资金削减已扰乱疫情 监测 与药品采购等关键职能,危及疟疾与结核病项目,并威胁增加发病率与 死亡率。抗疟药、结核病药物、抗逆转录病毒治疗药物、快速诊断试剂及个人防护装备的缺货可迅速将可控疾病转化为突发公共卫生事件。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将研究发现解读为当前埃博拉 暴发 是由冲突与人道主义紧缩驱动的更大协同流行的证据,强调需采用综合应对措施同时处理多重健康威胁。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明需采用综合策略加强卫生系统韧性,并确保对疾病防控项目的持续投资,特别是在多种传染病相互作用的冲突影响地区。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究受限于对报告数据的依赖,未纳入直接实证测量或统计分析。证据强度为中等,基于观察性数据与现有报告的推论。

analysis.time: The second meeting of the IHR Emergency Committee on the epidemic of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was held on 20 August 2026, with related news releases and statements published on 6 August 2026, 31 July 2026, and 24 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event is centered on the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically focusing on the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The affected population includes individuals in the DRC who are at risk of or have been exposed to the Bundibugyo virus.
analysis.event: The WHO and Africa CDC welcomed the allocation of Ebola vaccines to the DRC and called for urgent, community-led action to contain the Ebola outbreak. This is a statement regarding the ongoing epidemic of Bundibugyo virus disease in the DRC, confirmed by the WHO.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, which is a type of Ebola virus. The WHO has issued temporary recommendations to manage the epidemic, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided in the evidence. The risk is described as requiring urgent containment measures.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The WHO and Africa CDC are actively involved in the response, including vaccine allocation and calling for community-led actions. The recommendations are temporary, indicating that the situation is still under investigation and that further actions may be required.

analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC have welcomed the allocation of Ebola vaccines to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and called for urgent, community-led action to contain the ongoing epidemic of Bundibugyo virus disease. This follows a second meeting of the IHR Emergency Committee on the topic, held on 20 August 2026. The Bundibugyo virus is a member of the Ebola virus family, and the outbreak is currently being managed with temporary recommendations. While no specific case or death counts are provided in the evidence, the WHO has emphasized the need for immediate containment measures. The response includes vaccine distribution and collaboration with local communities to address the health emergency. The situation remains under investigation, and further actions may be required as the outbreak continues to be monitored.

elements_zh.time: 国际卫生条例(IHR)紧急委员会就刚果民主共和国丛林病毒病疫情召开第二次会议的时间为2026年8月20日,相关新闻稿及声明发布于2026年8月6日、2026年7月31日及2026年8月24日。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 该事件以刚果民主共和国(DRC)为中心,重点关注丛林病毒病暴发。受影响人群包括DRC境内面临或已暴露于丛林病毒的个体。
elements_zh.event: WHO与非洲疾控中心对向DRC分配埃博拉病毒疫苗疫苗表示欢迎,并呼吁采取紧急且以社区为主导的行动,以遏制DRC境内的埃博拉病毒病暴发。WHO已确认此为DRC境内丛林病毒病疫情,并发布相关声明。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 暴发涉及丛林病毒,其属于埃博拉病毒科。WHO已发布临时建议以应对疫情,但现有证据中未提供具体病例数、死亡数或暴露人数。WHO将该风险描述为需要紧急遏制措施。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: WHO与非洲疾控中心正积极参与应对,包括疫苗疫苗分配及倡导社区主导行动。由于建议为临时性,表明当前局势仍在调查中,可能需要进一步行动。

analysis_en.time: The second meeting of the IHR Emergency Committee on the epidemic of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was held on 20 August 2026, with related news releases and statements published on 6 August 2026, 31 July 2026, and 24 August 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The event is centered on the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically focusing on the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The affected population includes individuals in the DRC who are at risk of or have been exposed to the Bundibugyo virus.
analysis_en.event: The WHO and Africa CDC welcomed the allocation of Ebola vaccines to the DRC and called for urgent, community-led action to contain the Ebola outbreak. This is a statement regarding the ongoing epidemic of Bundibugyo virus disease in the DRC, confirmed by the WHO.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, which is a type of Ebola virus. The WHO has issued temporary recommendations to manage the epidemic, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided in the evidence. The risk is described as requiring urgent containment measures.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The WHO and Africa CDC are actively involved in the response, including vaccine allocation and calling for community-led actions. The recommendations are temporary, indicating that the situation is still under investigation and that further actions may be required.

news.title_zh: 世界卫生组织(WHO)——刚果民主共和国丛林病毒病疫情国际卫生条例(IHR)紧急委员会第二次会议:临时建议
news.source_body_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC have welcomed the allocation of Ebola vaccines to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and called for urgent, community-led action to contain the ongoing epidemic of Bundibugyo virus disease. This follows a second meeting of the IHR Emergency Committee on the topic, held on 20 August 2026. The Bundibugyo virus is a member of the Ebola virus family, and the outbreak is currently being managed with temporary recommendations. While no specific case or death counts are provided in the evidence, the WHO has emphasized the need for immediate containment measures. The response includes vaccine distribution and collaboration with local communities to address the health emergency. The situation remains under investigation, and further actions may be required as the outbreak continues to be monitored.

analysis.time: The outbreak is ongoing, with the latest updates published on 21 August 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the outbreak is described as a large outbreak in the DRC and Uganda.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. The affected population includes people in these regions, though specific demographic details are not provided in the evidence.
analysis.event: A large outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease is taking place in the DRC and Uganda. The event is reported by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), and it is confirmed as an ongoing outbreak.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 9 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 14 (10-16 August 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 21 Aug 2026 Originally published 21 Aug 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.38 MB) SITUATION OVERVIEW According to the World Health Organization, as of 16 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,001 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,378 deaths. With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, largescale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Given the high case fatality rate of 81% in internally displaced persons (IDP) sites, as per WHO and Africa CDC, a multisectoral response to multidimensional needs of displaced populations is critically required. The spread of the outbreak into Bas-Uélé Province underscores the continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. Community deaths account for over 50 per cent of fatalities as per government sources, indicating ongoing gaps in case detection and health-care seeking. Contact tracing is particularly weak in Bas-Uélé (18.9%), highlighting the need for continued disease surveillance and monitoring to ensure a complete epidemiological picture. The rapid geographic expansion of the outbreak creates additional needs for hygiene supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) consumables and health infrastructure, such as ambulances, to support timely prevention, detection, referral and response. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR). Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility continue to shape disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people in affected areas, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the rapidly escalating crisis, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts aim to enhance monitoring at points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs), particularly along the Congo River, to strengthen detection and response capacities. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries. IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of crossborder transmission. Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level. Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 9 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 14 (10-16 August 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 21 Aug 2026 Originally published 21 Aug 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.38 MB) SITUATION OVERVIEW According to the World Health Organization, as of 16 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,001 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,378 deaths. With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, largescale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Given the high case fatality rate of 81% in internally displaced persons (IDP) sites, as per WHO and Africa CDC, a multisectoral response to multidimensional needs of displaced populations is critically required. The spread of the outbreak into Bas-Uélé Province underscores the continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. Community deaths account for over 50 per cent of fatalities as per government sources, indicating ongoing gaps in case detection and health-care seeking. Contact tracing is particularly weak in Bas-Uélé (18.9%), highlighting the need for continued disease surveillance and monitoring to ensure a complete epidemiological picture. The rapid geographic expansion of the outbreak creates additional needs for hygiene supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) consumables and health infrastructure, such as ambulances, to support timely prevention, detection, referral and response. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR). Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility continue to shape disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people in affected areas, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the rapidly escalating crisis, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts aim to enhance monitoring at points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs), particularly along the Congo River, to strengthen detection and response capacities. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries. IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of crossborder transmission. Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level. news.content_zh: 国际移民组织(IOM)第14期疫情报告(2026年8月10日至16日)指出,刚果民主共和国(DRC)境内的布尼迪布焦病毒 暴发 疫情正在迅速升级,已成为该国规模最大且增长最快的疫情。截至8月16日,DRC报告确诊病例5,001例,死亡2,378例,其中社区死亡占总死亡人数的50%以上。该 暴发 已扩散至下韦莱省(Bas-Uélé),引发对向邻国(如南苏丹和中非共和国)跨境 传播 的担忧。IOM已扩大应对规模,重点加强关键入境点与控制点的监测,特别是沿刚果河一带。该 暴发 发生于东部DRC持续三重危机背景下,涉及健康风险、流离失所与冲突。下韦莱省的接触者追踪仍薄弱,需采取跨部门方法以满足流离失所人群的多重需求。报告强调持续开展疾病 监测 与加强区域协调的重要性,以减轻健康风险并确保及时预防与应对。

Español Key points CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Outbreak overview Risk to the United States To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States. The likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is considered very low. If a case was diagnosed in the United States, the risk of Ebola spreading in the United States is also low due to the strength of our public health system and infection control measures. CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus, in northeastern DRC and Uganda's capital Kampala. In DRC, cases have been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. This is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in DRC. This Ebola outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. In comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1,000 cases. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. The number of reported deaths has risen rapidly as well. All cases in Uganda so far have been diagnosed in its capital of Kampala, with no community spread reported. Uganda's last reported case, confirmed on June 21, was related to travel from DRC. The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's renewed August 12 order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. Latest data Reported cases This is a rapidly evolving situation, and case counts are subject to change. The DRC, Uganda, and France ministries of health (MOH) report the following: Skip Data Table Data table showing data for the table figure. The DRC MoH does not include probable cases in their official reporting. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. The Uganda MoH does not include suspected cases in their official reporting. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 500 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's renewed August 12 order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. Latest data Reported cases This is a rapidly evolving situation, and case counts are subject to change. The DRC MoH does not include probable cases in their official reporting. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. The Uganda MoH does not include suspected cases in their official reporting. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 500 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. This outbreak, which began in August 2026, is the second-largest on record and has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. No cases have been confirmed in the United States, and the risk of spreading to the U.S. is considered very low. news.source_body_en: The CDC is addressing an Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in remote regions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This outbreak, which began in August 2026, is the second-largest on record and has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. No cases have been confirmed in the United States, and the risk of spreading to the U.S. is considered very low. The outbreak is spreading faster than previous ones, with cases reported in several DRC provinces, including Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, and Tshopo. In Uganda, all cases have been diagnosed in Kampala, with no community spread reported. The response faces challenges due to limited healthcare infrastructure, ongoing conflict, and lack of public trust. To mitigate risks, the U.S. has temporarily restricted entry for travelers from DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan, requiring a 21-day quarantine period. Enhanced precautions are advised for those traveling to affected areas.
news.content_zh: 美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)正在应对由本迪布焦病毒(Bundibugyo virus)引发的埃博拉病毒病(Ebola 暴发)暴发,该暴发发生在刚果民主共和国(DRC)和乌干达的偏远地区。此次暴发始于2026年8月,是有记录以来第二大暴发,在响应行动启动后40天内确诊病例已超过1,000例。美国尚未确认任何病例,且疾病传入美国的风险被认为非常低。此次暴发的传播速度较以往更快,在DRC多个省份报告了病例,包括上乌埃莱省、伊图里省、北基伍省、南基伍省和特舒波省。在乌干达,所有病例均在坎帕拉市确诊,未报告社区传播。由于医疗基础设施有限、冲突持续和公众信任缺失,响应行动面临挑战。为降低风险,美国已暂时限制来自DRC、乌干达和南苏丹的旅客入境,并要求实施21天隔离。建议前往疫区的旅行者采取加强防护措施。

Preparing for future pandemics CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, is a global partnership working to accelerate the development of vaccines and other biologic countermeasures against epidemic and pandemic threats. Find out more Latest News Latest News See more Blog 100 days into the Bundibugyo emergency, unprecedented speed is still not enough News New studies to test whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses to Bundibugyo ebolavirus Explainer CEPI 3.0 cross-cutting themes explained: Biosecurity News CEPI Board appoints Ibrahim Abubakar as new Chief Executive Officer News CEPIâs Principles for Responding to Outbreaks Impact story How vaccine trials in Congo could help protect mothers and children from Mpox News African Institutions' Readiness to Conduct Phase 1 Bundibugyo Vaccine Trials News Modernaâs Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine candidate enters first human trial, backed by CEPI Explainer CEPI 3.0 explained: Networks News Hilleman Laboratories to develop and produce CEPI-backed Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine doses for clinical trials Latest News See more We want to create a world in which epidemics and pandemics are no longer a threat to humanity. CEPI is working to galvanise the development of new vaccines and other biologic countermeasures against diseases that could cause the next devastating epidemic or pandemic. Our approach Securing the Future CEPI 3.0 â our 2027-2031 strategy â aims to transform the worldâs ability to tackle epidemic and pandemic threats. Explore CEPIâs 3.0 Investment Case to see how we can #SecureTheFutureÂ together. Read more Research and development CEPI is leading a broad range of ambitious programmes that aim to substantially reduce global epidemic and pandemic risk. Read more Calls for Proposals Innovators worldwide are invited to apply to our scientific programmes to advance the development and manufacture of vaccines and tools against epidemic and pandemic threats. Read more Process development and manufacturing CEPI is bolstering global manufacturing capacity in underserved regions and harnessing innovative technologies to improve the speed, scale and access of vaccine manufacturing in response to epidemic and pandemic threats. Read more $12.5 trillion IMFâs estimate cost of the COVID-19 pandemic to the global economy through 2024 Over 75 Number of CEPI-supported vaccine candidates and platform technologies. 470+ R&D partners collaborating with CEPIâ ̄ Emerging infectious diseases affect us all. They do not respect borders. A commitment to equitable access informs every aspect of our work. It is core to CEPIâs vision of a world in which epidemics and pandemics are no longer a threat to humanity. CEPI take a systems approach to equitable access, seeking to enable equitable access within a broad ecosystem of national and international public and private sector partners and networks. We work towards this goal by enabling equitable access directly through financial investments and partnerships, and indirectly through advocacy and policy contributions to the evolving ecosystem. analysis.event: New studies are being conducted to test whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses to the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The event is reported by CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The studies aim to assess the effectiveness of existing vaccines against the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, which is a specific type of Ebola virus. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the research is part of broader efforts to prepare for future pandemics.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CEPI is actively working on vaccine development and countermeasures against epidemic and pandemic threats. The studies are part of their broader strategy to accelerate vaccine development. The evidence does not specify the current status of the investigation or testing, but it indicates ongoing efforts.

analysis.brief_en: CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, is conducting new studies to determine whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses to the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. This research is part of CEPI's broader strategy to prepare for future pandemics by accelerating the development of vaccines and other biologic countermeasures. The studies aim to evaluate the effectiveness of current vaccines against this specific strain of the virus. While no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence, the research is part of a global effort to reduce the risk of epidemic and pandemic threats. CEPI's approach includes financial investments, partnerships, and advocacy to ensure equitable access to vaccines and tools. The evidence does not specify the current status of the investigation or testing, but it highlights ongoing efforts to address emerging infectious diseases.

news.source_body_en: CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, is conducting new studies to determine whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses to the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. news.content_zh: 流行病防范创新联盟(CEPI)正在开展新研究,以确定现有埃博拉病毒疫苗是否能对邦迪布焦埃博拉病毒产生交叉保护。该研究是CEPI更广泛战略的一部分,旨在通过加速疫苗及其他生物制剂对策的研发,为应对未来大流行做准备。研究旨在评估当前疫苗对该病毒株的有效性。目前证据中未报告具体病例数、死亡数或暴露人数,但该研究是全球减少流行病和大流行威胁风险的一项努力。CEPI的方法包括财政投入、合作伙伴关系及倡导,以确保疫苗及工具的公平可及性。证据未说明当前调查或检测的具体状态,但强调了应对新发传染病的持续努力。
news.summary_zh: 流行病防范创新联盟(CEPI)正在开展新研究,以确定现有埃博拉病毒疫苗是否能对邦迪布焦埃博拉病毒产生交叉保护。该研究是CEPI更广泛战略的一部分,旨在通过加速疫苗及其他生物制剂对策的研发,为应对未来大流行做准备。研究旨在评估当前疫苗对该病毒株的有效性。目前证据中未报告具体病例数、死亡数或暴露人数,但该研究是全球减少流行病和大流行威胁风险的一项努力。CEPI的方法包括财政投入、合作伙伴关系及倡导,以确保疫苗及工具的公平可及性。证据未说明当前调查或检测的具体状态,但强调了应对新发传染病的持续努力。

news.content_title: Congo gambles on ‘old’ vaccine as new Ebola virus spirals
news.content: Congo is to try using an existing vaccine against its spiralling Ebola outbreak, even though the jab was developed to protect against a different strain of the virus. There is currently no specific vaccine to protect against the Bundibugyo, the strain of Ebola sweeping the north East of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). However, it has been given 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, a jab that has proven effective against the Zaire strain of the disease. Scientists hope it will provide at least some protection in the fastest ever outbreak of the deadly haemorrhagic fever while a new vaccine is developed. The outbreak has killed around 2,500 people, is doubling every 20 days , and is on track to be the largest ever known by around the end of September. The outbreak has so far killed 2,500 people and is doubling every 20 days - Luke Dray/Getty Images Europe Nearly half of all those infected have gone on to die. Dr Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine partnership, earlier this week said to beat the outbreak "we must deploy every tool at our disposal". She went on: "To avoid this becoming the worst recorded Ebola outbreak in history, it is critical that all effective countermeasure options are brought to bear. "We have a tool that could help save lives while we wait for [Bundibugyo]-specific vaccines to become available." Previous clinical trials have shown that Ervebo is safe, but its effect on other strains is unknown. The World Health Organisation said in a statement that while it was not known if Ervebo may protect against the Bundibugyo virus, "early laboratory and animal data suggest it may provide some protection". Medics told the Telegraph of anecdotal claims that health workers who had been given Ervebo to protect them during an outbreak of the Zaire strain in 2018 to 2020 had not fallen ill during the current Bundibugyo outbreak. Health workers are at extreme risk of catching the disease because they come into contact with highly-contagious blood, vomit and diarrhoea from dying patients. When they fall sick themselves, they frequently go on to infect their own families. Giving health workers vaccine jabs to protect them as they tend the sick is a cornerstone of Ebola responses. The WHO said the vaccine allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus. The remaining 50,000 doses will be used for front-line and health workers as recommended by WHO experts. Dr Nishtar said: "Having already been licensed for the Zaire strain, we know that Ervebo is proven to be safe. "And while the signs are that it may not stop transmission – which is essential for ending the outbreak - it could well save precious lives and reduce suffering." Health officials warn that the Bundibugyo outbreak centred on DRC's Ituri province is easily outpacing relief efforts . The virus is thought to have been spreading for months before an outbreak was finally declared in mid-May and medics have been unable to make up the head start. An analysis by the Africa Centres for Disease Control meanwhile warned the current outbreak dwarfed all others on record The current outbreak had almost ten times more cases than any other previous outbreak at a similar stage. analysis.brief_en: In the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), health officials are using the Ervebo vaccine, originally developed for the Zaire strain of Ebola, to combat a rapidly spreading Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Ituri province. The outbreak, which began in mid-May, has already claimed around 2,500 lives and is doubling every 20 days, potentially becoming the largest ever recorded by the end of September. While the World Health Organization (WHO) has allocated 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to assess the vaccine's effectiveness against the Bundibugyo strain, the remaining 50,000 doses are intended for front-line health workers, who are at high risk of infection due to exposure to contagious bodily fluids. Early laboratory and animal data suggest Ervebo may provide some protection, but its efficacy against the Bundibugyo virus remains unconfirmed. Health workers who were vaccinated during a previous Zaire strain outbreak in 2018-2020 reportedly did not contract the disease during the current Bundibugyo outbreak, though this is anecdotal. The WHO emphasizes that while the vaccine may not stop transmission, it could save lives and reduce suffering during the development of a specific vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain.

analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 本迪布焦病毒疫情已致约2,500人死亡,感染者死亡率接近50%。疫情每20天病例数量翻一番,预计到9月底将超过以往所有同类疫情规模。一线医护人员因接触传染性体液而面临极高感染风险。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: The WHO has allocated 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial and 50,000 doses for front-line health workers. The effectiveness of Ervebo against the Bundibugyo virus is not yet confirmed, and early laboratory and animal data suggest it may provide some protection. The outbreak is outpacing relief efforts, and no conclusions have been made about the vaccine's impact on the Bundibugyo virus.

GO TO SITE MSF Access CRASH Based in Paris, CRASH conducts and directs studies and analysis of MSF actions. They participate in internal training sessions and assessment missions in the field. GO TO SITE CRASH UREPH Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action. GO TO SITE UREPH ARHP Based in Barcelona, ARHP documents and reflects on the operational challenges and dilemmas faced by the MSF field teams. GO TO SITE ARHP MSF Analysis Based in Brussels, MSF Analysis intends to stimulate reflection and debate on humanitarian topics organised around the themes of migration, refugees, aid access, health policy and the environment in which aid operates. GO TO SITE MSF Analysis MSF Supply This logistical and supply centre in Brussels provides storage of and delivers medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Supply MSF Logistique This supply and logistics centre in Bordeaux, France, provides warehousing and delivery of medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Logistique Amsterdam Procurement Unit This logistical centre in Amsterdam purchases, tests, and stores equipment including vehicles, communications material, power supplies, water-processing facilities and nutritional supplements. GO TO SITE Amsterdam Procurement Unit Brazilian Medical Unit BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. GO TO SITE Brazilian Medical Unit MSF Medical Guidelines Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals. GO TO SITE MSF Medical Guidelines Epicentre Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care. GO TO SITE Epicentre Evaluation Units Evaluation Units have been established in Vienna, Stockholm, and Paris, assessing the potential and limitations of medical humanitarian action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of our medical humanitarian work. GO TO SITE Evaluation Units LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population. GO TO SITE LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings LUXOR The Luxembourg Operational Research (LuxOR) unit coordinates field research projects and operational research training, and provides support for documentation activities and routine data collection. GO TO SITE LUXOR Intersectional Benchmarking Unit The Intersectional Benchmarking Unit collects and analyses data about local labour markets in all locations where MSF employs people. GO TO SITE Intersectional Benchmarking Unit MSF Academy for Healthcare To upskill and provide training to locally-hired MSF staff in several countries, MSF has created the MSF Academy for Healthcare. GO TO SITE MSF Academy for Healthcare Humanitarian Law This Guide explains the terms, concepts, and rules of humanitarian law in accessible and reader-friendly alphabetical entries. GO TO SITE Humanitarian Law MSF Paediatric Days The MSF Paediatric Days is an event for paediatric field staff, policy makers and academia to exchange ideas, align efforts, inspire and share frontline research to advance urgent paediatric issues of direct concern for the humanitarian field. GO TO SITE MSF Paediatric Days MSF Foundation The MSF Foundation aims to create a fertile arena for logistics and medical knowledge-sharing to meet the needs of MSF and the humanitarian sector as a whole. GO TO SITE MSF Foundation DNDi A collaborative, patients’ needs-driven, non-profit drug research and development organisation that is developing new treatments for neglected diseases, founded in 2003 by seven organisations from around the world. GO TO SITE DNDi MSF Science Portal Our digital portal dedicated to sharing the latest medical evidence from our humanitarian activities around the globe. GO TO SITE MSF Science Portal Noma Noma is a preventable and treatable neglected disease, but 90 per cent of people will die within the first two weeks of infection if they do not receive treatment. GO TO SITE Noma TIC The TIC is aiming to change how MSF works to better meet the evolving needs of our patients. GO TO SITE TIC Telemedicine MSF's telemedicine hub aims to overcome geographic barriers for equitable, accessible, and quality patient care. GO TO SITE Telemedicine Sweden Innovation Unit Launched in 2012, the MSF Sweden Innovation Unit deploys a human-centered approach for promoting a culture of innovation within MSF. GO TO SITE Sweden Innovation Unit Geo MSF The GeoMSF platform is a dynamic one-stop-shop website for all of MSF's GIS related services and products. Access maps and applications through the catalogue, request geographical support, or produce a map on GeoMSF. GeoMSF Geo MSF View Resource Centre Bangladesh Children arrive sicker, later, and harder to save at MSF’s Kutupalong hospital in Rohingya camps At Kutupalong hospital, a medical team, led by Dr Dolores Echezarreta, provides emergency care to Aiyan Arfan, who is 10-days-old. The team is working together to stabilise the infant’s health condition. Bangladesh, August 2026. © Nazmul Islam/MSF Project Update 25 Aug 2026 Rohingya families living in camps in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, struggle to secure basic food, healthcare, and education, placing children’s daily survival at constant risk. Read more Share An international, independent medical humanitarian organisation We provide medical assistance to people affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or exclusion from healthcare. Our teams are made up of tens of thousands of health professionals, logistic and administrative staff - most of them hired locally. Our actions are guided by medical ethics and the principles of impartiality, independence and neutrality. In Focus Gaza-Israel war Learn how MSF teams are responding to the genocide in Gaza, Palestine. In Focus Attacks on medical care Attacks against medical facilities and health workers, whether deliberate or indiscriminate, are part of generalised violence and atrocities committed against civilians in armed conflict. They deprive populations of health services, often when they need them the most. In Focus Conflict in Sudan Find out the latest information on MSF's response to the conflict in Sudan. In Focus Mediterranean migration Every year, thousands of people fleeing war, persecution and poverty at home attempt the treacherous journey across the Mediterranean. Countless lives are lost on the way. In Focus Rohingya refugee crisis Legally stateless, with very limited options or rights in any country where they have sought refuge, the Rohingya are extremely vulnerable. view more video Welcome to Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders Working with MSF What's it like to work with MSF? We rely on a strong network of professionals to deliver life-saving medical aid. Each year, thousands of international and locally-hired staff work together around the globe to provide lifesaving medical assistance to people who would otherwise be denied access to healthcare. Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to battle the outbreak caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. byMariam Ileyemi August 21, 2026 Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Add us on Google The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) has committed $4.17 million to four research projects examining whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses against the Bundibugyo virus. Join the Premium Times WhatsApp Community For Quick Access To News and Happenings Around You. Open in WhatsApp The studies, according to a news release on the CEPI website, will analyse stored blood samples from thousands of people previously vaccinated against Zaire ebolavirus, including recipients of the Ervebo vaccine. This will help to determine whether the vaccines could offer some protection against the different Ebola virus species. The research comes as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to battle the outbreak caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. Stay Ahead with Premium Times Follow us on Google News and never miss breaking stories, investigations, and in-depth reporting. Add as a preferred source on Google The World Health Organisation (WHO) on Wednesday declared the ongoing outbreak in the country the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. According to WHO’s latest disease outbreak update, 4,665 confirmed cases and 2,184 deaths have been recorded across five provinces and 54 health zones. WHO also declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May. No licensed Bundibugyo vaccine According to the CEO of CEPI, Richard Hatchett, there is currently no licensed vaccine specifically approved for Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease. Hatchett said Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates are being developed but would not be available during the earliest phase of the current outbreak. “However, vaccines do exist for the related Zaire ebolavirus, including Ervebo. Given the recent announcement that Ervebo will be deployed for emergency use against Bundibugyo virus, these CEPI-backed studies will be all the more important to inform on how we can make the best use of the existing vaccine,” he said. CEPI noted that the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritisation has recommended that Ervebo be evaluated in a phase three clinical trial alongside Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates when they become available. It added that the DRC authorities and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention have also announced plans to deploy Ervebo to priority groups under a protocol-governed expanded-use arrangement. Research to guide vaccine decisions CEPI said the projects were selected through its June 2026 call for proposals aimed at generating evidence for Bundibugyo vaccine research and development. The organisation said the studies would help address gaps in knowledge about the potential use of existing vaccines against the virus and support decisions on vaccination during the current outbreak and future responses. The funding is supported by the European Commission through a 2026 Horizon Europe grant, the United States Department of State and CEPI’s “existing core funding.” What the studies will examine CEPI said the four projects will focus on understanding whether vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus can trigger antibody responses that recognise Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The studies will also help establish and standardise antibody tests for Bundibugyo virus and examine how long such immune responses last. “Researchers will undertake antibody testing against all Orthoebolavirus species and Marburg virus, prioritising tests for Bundibugyo ebolavirus. They will examine which vaccines potentially provide cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus and identify vaccination regimens that might be associated with broad and durable cross-reactive immune responses,” CEPI noted. “Part of the award will transfer these laboratory methods to INRB in DRC, harmonising their laboratory capacity with that of CEPI’s Centralised Laboratory Network and international antibody reference standards. First antibody results are expected within two to six months.” Institutions involved CEPI added that the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Fielding School of Public Health will receive $2.05 million for its study. The researchers will examine blood samples from more than 1,700 people who received Ervebo and another Ebola vaccine. The Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp will receive $1.02 million for its EBO-BOOST-BRIDGE project, which will study samples from more than 600 participants. READ ALSO: WHO raises Ebola risk level as DRC outbreak worsens, reports new hantavirus cases CEPI said the project would also transfer laboratory methods to the National Institute of Biomedical Research in the DRC, with the first results expected within two to six months. The University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine’s Centre for Human Genetics and Pandemic Sciences Institute will receive $975,000 to study blood samples from people who received Ervebo and survivors of Zaire ebolavirus disease. The study will examine whether immunity from vaccination or previous infection could potentially protect against Bundibugyo virus. The MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research will receive $120,000 to study samples from vaccinated close contacts and Ugandan healthcare workers. The researchers will determine whether antibodies generated by Ervebo also recognise Bundibugyo virus. analysis.time: The research comes as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to battle the outbreak caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus (N1, N6). The publication date is August 21, 2026 (N2).
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically across five provinces and 54 health zones (N9).
analysis.event: CEPI has committed $4.17 million to study whether existing Ebola vaccines can generate immune responses against the Bundibugyo virus (N1, N2). The event is confirmed based on the news release and official statements (N1, N2).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The DRC outbreak has recorded 4,665 confirmed cases and 2,184 deaths (N9). The outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May (N10). The studies will examine blood samples from more than 1,700 people who received Ervebo and another Ebola vaccine (N25).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CEPI-backed studies are underway to analyse stored blood samples from vaccinated individuals (N4, N25). The DRC authorities and Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention have announced plans to deploy Ervebo to priority groups under a protocol-governed expanded-use arrangement (N16).

analysis.brief_en: CEPI has committed $4.17 million to study whether existing Ebola vaccines can offer protection against the Bundibugyo virus, which is currently causing a significant outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The outbreak, declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May, has resulted in 4,665 confirmed cases and 2,184 deaths across five provinces and 54 health zones. The research will examine blood samples from over 1,700 people who received the Ervebo vaccine and another Ebola vaccine. CEPI’s initiative aims to determine the effectiveness of these vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus, which does not yet have a licensed vaccine. The DRC authorities and Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention have also announced plans to deploy Ervebo to priority groups under an expanded-use protocol. Home News Science CEPI-backed studies to assess Ebola vaccine response against Bundibugyo ebolavirus Researchers will analyse immune responses in previously vaccinated people to determine whether existing Ebola vaccines could offer protection against the related virus. By Our Bureau Updated - August 20, 2026 at 09:20 PM. GIFT THIS ARTICLE This is a premium feature available only to paid subscribers of businessline Subscribe × Share WhatsAppXFacebookLinkedInMessengerRedditMail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/science/cepi-backed-studies-to-assess-ebola-vaccine-response-against-bundibugyo-ebolavirus/article71370328.eceCopy CEPI is funding four research projects to assess whether vaccines licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, including Ervebo, could provide protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. New studies are underway to assess if vaccines licensed against the Zaire ebolavirus—including Ervebo—could offer protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus, the virus behind the rapidly escalating outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The studies are supported by the international organisation CEPI – the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is providing $4.17 million to four research projects conducting them. The Ebola outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in May 2026. The four awardees undertaking the study include research groups led by UCLA (USA), the Institute of Tropical Medicine (Antwerp), the University of Oxford (UK), and the MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research (UK). “There is no licensed vaccine against Bundibugyo virus. CEPI is funding multiple Bundibugyo vaccine candidates to address this gap, but even on the most compressed timelines those vaccines will not be available for the earliest phase of this outbreak”, said Dr Richard Hatchett, CEPI Chief Executive Officer. “However, vaccines do exist for the related Zaire ebolavirus, including Ervebo. Given the recent announcement that Ervebo will be deployed for emergency use against Bundibugyo virus, these CEPI-backed studies will be all the more important to inform on how we can make the best use of the existing vaccine,” he added. Explaining how it would work, CEPI said research teams will analyse stored blood samples from individuals vaccinated with licensed/previously licensed vaccines against Zaire ebolavirus either in previous vaccination campaigns and/or clinical trials. They aim to characterise vaccine-induced immune responses and assess cross-reactivity of antibody responses against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The critical data that these serology studies will provide will help establish and standardise tests for antibodies against Bundibugyo virus and use longitudinal samples to define the dynamics and durability of these responses, it explained. Data from these studies will also aid interpretation of immune responses in clinical trials, help assess whether Bundibugyo-specific antibodies are associated with protection, and inform future vaccination strategies and evaluation of Bundibugyo-specific and broadly protective filovirus vaccines, CEPI said. Home News Science CEPI-backed studies to assess Ebola vaccine response against Bundibugyo ebolavirus Researchers will analyse immune responses in previously vaccinated people to determine whether existing Ebola vaccines could offer protection against the related virus. By Our Bureau Updated - August 20, 2026 at 09:20 PM. GIFT THIS ARTICLE This is a premium feature available only to paid subscribers of businessline Subscribe × Share WhatsAppXFacebookLinkedInMessengerRedditMail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/science/cepi-backed-studies-to-assess-ebola-vaccine-response-against-bundibugyo-ebolavirus/article71370328.eceCopy CEPI is funding four research projects to assess whether vaccines licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, including Ervebo, could provide protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. New studies are underway to assess if vaccines licensed against the Zaire ebolavirus—including Ervebo—could offer protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus, the virus behind the rapidly escalating outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The studies are supported by the international organisation CEPI – the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is providing $4.17 million to four research projects conducting them. The Ebola outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in May 2026. The four awardees undertaking the study include research groups led by UCLA (USA), the Institute of Tropical Medicine (Antwerp), the University of Oxford (UK), and the MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research (UK). “There is no licensed vaccine against Bundibugyo virus. CEPI is funding multiple Bundibugyo vaccine candidates to address this gap, but even on the most compressed timelines those vaccines will not be available for the earliest phase of this outbreak”, said Dr Richard Hatchett, CEPI Chief Executive Officer. “However, vaccines do exist for the related Zaire ebolavirus, including Ervebo. Given the recent announcement that Ervebo will be deployed for emergency use against Bundibugyo virus, these CEPI-backed studies will be all the more important to inform on how we can make the best use of the existing vaccine,” he added. Explaining how it would work, CEPI said research teams will analyse stored blood samples from individuals vaccinated with licensed/previously licensed vaccines against Zaire ebolavirus either in previous vaccination campaigns and/or clinical trials. They aim to characterise vaccine-induced immune responses and assess cross-reactivity of antibody responses against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The critical data that these serology studies will provide will help establish and standardise tests for antibodies against Bundibugyo virus and use longitudinal samples to define the dynamics and durability of these responses, it explained. Data from these studies will also aid interpretation of immune responses in clinical trials, help assess whether Bundibugyo-specific antibodies are associated with protection, and inform future vaccination strategies and evaluation of Bundibugyo-specific and broadly protective filovirus vaccines, CEPI said. news.source_body_en: CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, is funding four research projects to evaluate whether existing vaccines against Zaire ebolavirus, such as Ervebo, could offer protection against the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. These studies aim to characterise immune responses in individuals previously vaccinated against Zaire ebolavirus and assess cross-reactivity of antibodies against Bundibugyo. The research will help establish tests for Bundibugyo-specific antibodies and define the durability of immune responses. CEPI has stated that while no licensed vaccine exists for Bundibugyo, existing vaccines may be useful in the early stages of the outbreak. The studies are part of broader efforts to develop vaccines for this virus, which has been linked to a rapidly escalating outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. news.content_zh: 流行病防范创新联盟(CEPI)正在资助四个研究项目,以评估现有针对扎伊尔埃博拉病毒的疫苗(如 Ervebo)是否能为布迪布焦埃博拉病毒提供保护。这些研究旨在表征先前接种过扎伊尔埃博拉病毒疫苗的个体中的免疫应答,并评估抗体对布迪布焦病毒的交叉反应性。该研究将帮助建立布迪布焦病毒特异性抗体检测,并界定免疫应答的持久性。CEPI 表示,尽管目前尚无针对布迪布焦病毒的获批疫苗,现有疫苗或可在该病毒暴发的早期阶段发挥作用。这些研究是更广泛努力的一部分,旨在为该病毒开发疫苗,该病毒已与刚果民主共和国迅速升级的暴发相关。研究结果将为未来疫苗接种策略及广谱保护性丝状病毒疫苗的评估提供依据。
